title: Guillain–Barre Syndrome following lower segment caesarean section under spinal anesthesia: A case report
case_prompt:
A 27-year-old primiparous woman underwent an emergency lower-segment cesarean section under spinal anesthesia at 38 weeks’ gestation for fetal distress. She was discharged on postoperative day 5 with only mild numbness and tingling in her lower limbs. On postoperative day 22, she was readmitted with a 2-week history of progressive weakness in both upper and lower limbs, which began insidiously on day 8 after surgery. The weakness was symmetric, progressed from distal to proximal, and initially allowed her to perform daily activities with assistance, but by day 22 she could no longer stand or support herself. She also noted burning and tingling sensations in her lower limbs with reduced touch perception. She denied dysphagia, dysarthria, visual changes, headache, photophobia, double vision, abnormal movements, loss of consciousness, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. There was no preceding gastrointestinal or respiratory illness and no relevant medical, surgical, or vaccination history.

On examination, her temperature was normal, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 100/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Higher mental functions and cranial nerves were intact. Muscle bulk and tone were normal. Strength testing revealed 5/5 strength in shoulder abduction and adduction, elbow flexion and extension, and wrist movements; hand grip strength was 80% of normal. In the lower limbs, hip flexion and extension and hip abduction/adduction were 2/5, knee flexion and extension were 0/5, and toe movements were 0/5. Reflexes were 2+ at the biceps and triceps, absent at the knees and ankles, and plantar responses were downgoing bilaterally. Sensation to touch, pinprick, and vibration was intact in all limbs.

Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 71.6 mg/dL, a total white-cell count of <5 mononuclear cells, glucose 64 mg/dL, adenosine deaminase 4.8 U/L (normal 0–30 U/L), no red cells, and no growth on culture after 48 hours. Nerve conduction studies revealed a generalized severe sensory polyneuropathy and axonopathy of the bilateral posterior tibial nerves. A noncontrast CT scan of the head and MRI of the cervical spine were unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Guillain–Barré syndrome was considered because of the progressive, symmetrical limb weakness, albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF, and axonal neuropathy on nerve conduction studies — “According to these findings, acute motor‐sensory axonal neuropathy variant of GBS was considered.”
2. Transverse myelitis was ruled out by the absence of upper motor neuron signs and normal spinal imaging — “Absence of upper motor signs, insignificant MRI findings… helped to rule out possibility of transverse myelitis.”
3. Lumbar epidural hematoma was excluded due to lack of focal lesions on imaging — “insignificant MRI findings… helped to rule out possibility of lumbar epidural hematoma.”
4. Poliomyelitis was considered unlikely given the presence of sensory symptoms and nerve conduction study findings of a polyneuropathy — “symmetrical weakness with presence of sensory symptoms and NCT findings helped to rule out possibility of… poliomyelitis respectively.”
